title: Muhammad Iqbal
hook: the poet-philosopher of South Asia who urged the self to rise

segments.voice: Yesterday, the reformers, al-Afghani and Abduh, calling for renewal through schools and reason. Your line was: renewal. Which stale habit did you do as if for the first time? Today, renewal written as poetry. Day one thousand twenty-two.

A schoolyard in India. Children line up in the morning and sing a song that begins, in Urdu, with the claim that their land is better than all the world. A wedding in Lahore, and someone recites a couplet about the falcon who refuses to build a nest. A seminar room, and a professor lectures on how the Qur'an speaks of the human self. Three places, three audiences, and the same author behind all of them: a poet who studied law and philosophy, wrote poetry in two languages, and kept asking what a human being is capable of. Today: Muhammad Iqbal.
screen: `A SONG IN A SCHOOLYARD.` → `A FALCON AT A WEDDING.` → `ONE POET BEHIND THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: Iqbal grew up in the Punjab, studied in Lahore, and then in England and Germany. He came home a philosopher, a lawyer, and above all a poet, writing in Urdu and in Persian. His great word was khudi. It means selfhood, the self. Not selfishness. For Iqbal, khudi was the spark God placed in each person, meant to be strengthened, not dissolved. He looked around at Muslims under colonial rule and saw people who had learned to make themselves small: waiting, imitating, apologizing. His poetry kept saying the opposite. Rise. One often-quoted couplet, in paraphrase, goes like this: raise your selfhood so high that, before each turn of destiny, God himself asks the servant, tell me, what do you wish? Bold words, and Iqbal meant them boldly. But the self he praised is not a self without God. It grows strong by drawing near to God, the way a flame grows by being fed. A bird he returns to again and again is the falcon, a creature of the high air that, in his verse, will not settle for an easy nest. Behind this stands a line of the Qur'an. In surah at-Tin, in Pickthall's words: "Surely We created man of the best stature." Some readers hear Iqbal's idea in it: a dignity to grow into. Readers disagree about him, too. Some hear a poet of spiritual courage. Others focus on his politics, or argue over how far his philosophy strays from the old scholars. Pakistan honors him, and his songs are still sung in India. The self can rise.
screen: `A POET IN URDU AND PERSIAN.` · `KHUDI: SELFHOOD, NOT SELFISHNESS.` · `GOD ASKS: WHAT DO YOU WISH?` · `THE FALCON WON'T SETTLE.` · then, large: `SURELY WE CREATED MAN OF THE BEST STATURE.`

segments.voice: The practice: write one line of hope, starting with finding it now. Settle, and breathe. If there's a place in your life where you make yourself small, waiting for permission, apologizing for taking up room, bring it to mind. Now ask: what would rising look like there? Not shouting. Just standing a little taller. Let a sentence form. It doesn't need to rhyme. It only needs to be true and hopeful. If you pray, you can hold the words of surah at-Tin, of the best stature. If not, just hold your line. The bell holds the time.
Muhammad Iqbal. The poet-philosopher of South Asia who taught khudi, selfhood, and urged the self to rise toward God. Today's word.
Your line: the self can rise. Today, write your one line of hope down, and put it somewhere you'll see it tonight. Day one thousand twenty-two.

howItsDone: Iqbal's poems are recited and sung in Urdu and Persian at gatherings, in schools and in qawwali, and his lines are often quoted in sermons and speeches across South Asia.

notes: Editor pass: removed unsourced superlatives ('the best-known couplet', 'his favorite bird'); the claim that Iqbal himself read 95:4 this way is now offered as what some readers hear; practice no longer assumes the listener makes themselves small.
The khudi couplet ('Khudi ko kar buland itna...') is paraphrased; confirm the paraphrase and its source collection (Bal-e-Jibril).

The schoolyard song is Saare Jahan Se Achha (Tarana-e-Hind); the script says it 'begins with the claim that their land is better than all the world'. Confirm, and confirm it is still sung in Indian schools.
Falcon (shaheen) imagery in Iqbal: confirm the 'refuses to build a nest' paraphrase.
Biography: Punjab, Lahore, England and Germany; law and philosophy. Confirm. No dates given.
'Pakistan honors him': he is Pakistan's national poet; confirm wording.
Nicholson's 1920 translation of Asrar-i-Khudi is likely public domain, but no line was quoted from it.
Pickthall 95:4 quoted from memory, matching wording used elsewhere in this path; confirm.
